faqs.question: Which Halloween movie quotes are in the public domain?
faqs.answer: In the US, lines from films released before 1931, such as Nosferatu (1922) and The Phantom of the Opera (1925), are public domain, and so is Night of the Living Dead (1968), which was released without a copyright notice. Lines from those films can be printed word for word with the film and year credited.

faqs.question: When do Dracula and Frankenstein become public domain?
faqs.answer: Both 1931 Universal films are protected through 31 December 2026 and enter the US public domain on 1 January 2027, because pre-1978 works get 95 years ending on 1 January after the 95th year. Sequels such as Bride of Frankenstein (1935) run on their own later clocks.

faqs.question: Why is Night of the Living Dead in the public domain?
faqs.answer: When the distributor changed the title from Night of the Flesh Eaters, the copyright notice was dropped from the prints. Under US rules for works published from 1931 to 1977, release without a notice meant the film entered the public domain on release.

faqs.question: Is Nosferatu free to quote?
faqs.answer: The 1922 film is in the US public domain because it was released before 1931. The English intertitles you see depend on the print, and a modern restoration can carry a newly copyrighted translation, so quote from an old print or translate the German original yourself.

faqs.question: Can I put a horror movie quote on a T-shirt I sell?
faqs.answer: A line from a public-domain film is safer than a modern one, but merchandise also raises trademark questions: the US Copyright Office notes that short phrases, while not copyrightable, may be protected under trademark law. For anything you sell, check trademarks and take proper legal advice.

faqs.question: Can I use a modern horror movie line in an Instagram caption?
faqs.answer: The US Copyright Office says words and short phrases are not copyrightable, so a few words in a caption are a different matter from reprinting a scene. This page still names modern films and describes the moment instead of printing their lines, and longer exchanges of dialogue are protected script.

faqs.question: What is the famous line from Halloween (1978)?
faqs.answer: The line people repeat comes early in John Carpenter's 1978 film, when the sheriff remarks that Halloween night entitles everyone to a fright. The film is in copyright for decades, so watch it for the exact wording rather than copying it from a list.

faqs.question: Can I use the 40 original lines on this page?
faqs.answer: Yes. All 40 lines in the slasher, haunted house, creature feature, witchy and 1950s B-movie sets were written for this page and are not taken from any film, so they need no credit.

faqs.question: Which movie-style lines suit a kids' Halloween card?
faqs.answer: The witchy and campy 1950s B-movie sets are the gentlest; skip the slasher set for children. The Halloween card template has a kids tone with no blood, no gore and no jump scares, which suits those lines.

faqs.question: Why do people love quoting horror movies?
faqs.answer: One explanation is practice: in a study of 310 US adults surveyed in April 2020, horror fans were more resilient during the COVID-19 pandemic, and fans of zombie and other prepper genres were also better prepared. The design is correlational, so it shows an association, not a cause.

faqs.question: Does public domain in the US mean public domain everywhere?
faqs.answer: No. Many countries, including those in the EU, use a life-plus-70-year term, so a film that is free to quote in the US can still be protected elsewhere. Check the rules where you will use the quote.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Movie Quotes You Can Actually Copy, Film by Film

The Halloween movie quotes you can print word for word come from films in the US public domain: silents released before 1931, such as *Nosferatu* (1922), plus *Night of the Living Dead* (1968), which lost its copyright notice. Format matters too: 48.3% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, and the average page is viewed 11.1 times, so a line must survive a small screen and a second read. Below: 10 verified lines from five public-domain films, the *Dracula* and *Frankenstein* (1931) scenes that unlock on 1 January 2027, modern moments described, and 40 original lines.

## What makes a Halloween movie quote safe to copy?

A public-domain movie quote is a line from a film whose US copyright has expired or never attached, so anyone may reprint it. For films released before 1978, the [Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain](https://web.law.duke.edu/cspd/publicdomainday/2026/) gives the maths: 95 years, ending on 1 January after the 95th year.

That frees every film from 1930 or earlier. The [Cornell University Library copyright chart](https://guides.library.cornell.edu/copyright/publicdomain) adds a second route: US works published from 1931 to 1977 without a copyright notice lost protection on release.

| Film | Year | US public-domain status | What you may quote |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Nosferatu* | 1922 | Public domain: pre-1931 | Any intertitle, from an old print or your own translation |
| *The Phantom of the Opera* | 1925 | Public domain: pre-1931 | Any intertitle, 1925 cut or 1929 reissue |
| *Dracula*, *Frankenstein* | 1931 | Protected to 31 Dec 2026; public domain 1 Jan 2027 | Nothing verbatim before 2027 |
| *Night of the Living Dead* | 1968 | Public domain: no copyright notice | Any line of dialogue |
| *Halloween* | 1978 | Protected; public domain no earlier than 2074 | Describe the scene only |

The line between "free" and "ask first" falls on a date. Every 1 January it moves forward one year.

## 10 Halloween movie quotes from public-domain films

Each line comes from a pre-1931 film or *Night of the Living Dead*. Quote it as written and credit film and year.

### 1. *Nosferatu* (1922)

F. W. Murnau's German silent predates 1931. English intertitles vary; a restoration's new translation can carry its own copyright, so use an old print or translate the German.

- "Is this your wife? What a lovely throat!" (Count Orlok)
- "Blood is life! Blood is life!" (Knock, the estate agent)
- "We will go no further. Here begins the land of phantoms." (the coachmen)

### 2. *Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde* (1920)

John Barrymore's American silent needs no translation. Its best-known card is lifted from Oscar Wilde's *The Picture of Dorian Gray* (1890).

- "The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it." (intertitle)

### 3. *The Phantom of the Opera* (1925)

Lon Chaney's Phantom premiered in New York on 6 September 1925. The lines follow [Wikiquote's transcription](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/The_Phantom_of_the_Opera_(1925_film)); check them against your print.

- "Feast your eyes! Glut your soul on my accursed ugliness!" (the Phantom, unmasked)
- "Beneath your dancing feet are the tombs of tortured men!" (the Phantom, as the Red Death)
- "Look not upon my mask — think rather of my devotion which has brought you the gift of song." (the Phantom, to Christine)

### 4. *The Bat Whispers* (1930)

This early talkie entered the US public domain on 1 January 2026, with all of 1930. It is more mystery than horror.

- "The entire police force won't do no good. They can't stop ghosts." (the caretaker)

### 5. *Night of the Living Dead* (1968)

The distributor dropped the copyright notice when it retitled the film from *Night of the Flesh Eaters*, per [Wikipedia's account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_of_the_Living_Dead). Before 1978, no notice meant no copyright.

- "They're coming to get you, Barbra!" (Johnny, teasing his sister)
- "Don't you know what's goin' on out there? This is no Sunday School picnic!" (Ben)

## Dracula and Frankenstein become quotable on 1 January 2027

*Dracula* premiered in New York on 12 February 1931, and *Frankenstein* followed later that year. Both stay protected through 31 December 2026; Duke's own example of a 1931 work waiting until 2027 is *Mood Indigo*.

These four scenes become quotable word for word on 1 January 2027. Until then, describe them.

- Bela Lugosi's slow self-introduction on the cobwebbed staircase.
- His reply when he pours Renfield wine and declines a glass himself.
- Colin Clive's repeated cry in the laboratory as the creature's hand moves.
- The boast that follows, about knowing how it feels to be God.

Sequels such as *Bride of Frankenstein* (1935) keep their own clocks, and trademarks can still cover a character on merchandise. Stoker's 1897 novel, source of the "children of the night" line, is already free.

## Modern Halloween movies: the moments people quote

Newer films stay protected for decades, so here is the moment people repeat, not the line. The US Copyright Office's [Circular 33](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ33.pdf) (revised March 2021) says short phrases are not copyrightable but may fall under trademark law, while longer exchanges are protected script.

- *Halloween* (1978): the sheriff granting everyone a fright on Halloween night.
- *The Shining* (1980): Jack's grin through the splintered door.
- *Poltergeist* (1982): Carol Anne at the static-filled television.
- *Beetlejuice* (1988): the name you never say three times.
- *Hocus Pocus* (1993): Winifred urging her sisters to run riot through Salem.
- *Scream* (1996): the phone call asking about your favourite scary movie.

## 40 original movie-style Halloween lines, by genre

Every line here is original to this page, so use it without credit. In [a study of 310 US adults surveyed in April 2020](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7492010), horror fans were more resilient during the pandemic, and fans of zombie and other "prepper" genres were also better prepared; the authors read scary fiction as safe practice, though the design is correlational.

### Slasher lines (8)

- The porch bulb blinked twice, and we had already unscrewed it.
- He doesn't run. He never has to run.
- The babysitter counted the kids at nine. At ten she counted again.
- Every mask in this town has a face behind it, and one of them is smiling.
- Don't split up, don't go to the basement, and don't trust the quiet.
- The candy bowl was full when we left. Now there's a note in it.
- Thirty-one days of October, and he only needs one night.
- The last kid on the street always takes the shortcut through the woods.

### Haunted house lines (8)

- The house sold three times in one year. The furniture never moved out.
- Every door upstairs is locked from the inside.
- Grandmother's portrait used to face the window.
- The staircase has thirteen steps going up and fourteen coming down.
- We bought the house for the garden. The house bought us for the attic.
- Nobody lives on the third floor, yet someone still asks for breakfast.
- The piano plays at 3 a.m., and it's always the same four notes.
- The previous owners left one rule taped to the fridge: don't answer the knock.

### Creature feature lines (8)

- Something in the lake has learned to count the rowing boats.
- The full moon is tomorrow, Doctor. Lock the cage tonight.
- Footprints this size don't belong to anything on the map.
- Don't shine the torch at it. It likes the light.
- The village has one law after dark: bolt the shutters and don't whistle.
- Fur on the fence, mud on the stairs, and the dog won't stop staring at the ceiling.
- Whatever it is, it's taller than the barn.
- Every legend starts with a farmer nobody believed.

### Witchy lines (8)

- Three drops of moonlight, a pinch of spite and your name spelled backwards.
- The coven meets at midnight. Bring your own broom and your best excuse.
- I didn't curse the village. I simply stopped un-cursing it.
- Mind the cat. She's older than the church.
- Every herb in my garden is either medicine or a warning.
- She stirred the cauldron clockwise, and the whole town forgot her name.
- Never borrow a witch's ladle and return it dirty.
- A hex is just a short word for "you should have apologised".

### Campy 1950s B-movie lines (8)

- Attention, citizens of Pine Hollow: the meteor has landed, and it wants pie.
- Great galloping galaxies, the pumpkins are multiplying!
- Professor, your experiment has escaped, and it's wearing your hat.
- Stay in your cars! The fifty-foot scarecrow is heading for the drive-in!
- They're not monsters, Sheriff. They're teenagers in rubber suits. Probably.
- Science has no explanation for the glowing gelatin.
- Lock up the radio station, Marge, the Martians want the request line.
- On the stroke of twelve the mummy walks, and he's asking for directions.

## Putting one movie line on a Halloween page for one person

A quote lands harder inside something the person opens. The [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) lets you write a letter they read by flashlight in a dark attic, choose the word they carve into a jack-o'-lantern, and end on a question of up to 60 characters.

A witchy line fits the letter, PHANTOMS the pumpkin, and "Will you haunt the drive-in with me on the 31st?" the question. Its kids mode has no blood, gore or jump scares, so use witchy or B-movie lines there.

The [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a voice note of up to 60 seconds, enough to read the Phantom's unmasking card aloud. Across the platform, 38.5% of creators password-protect a page before sharing it.

## When a movie quote is the wrong choice

Public domain here means the United States. Duke notes that EU countries and many others use life-plus-70 terms, so a US-free film may be protected elsewhere.

Merchandise is the second trap. Circular 33 points short phrases toward trademark law, and studio monsters keep trademarks after copyright ends, so a shirt needs more care than a caption.

The page greets one person, not a party crowd, and its interface is English. For someone who has seen *Night of the Living Dead* ten times, watching it with them may beat any quote.

## Sources

- Jenkins and Boyle, [Public Domain Day 2026](https://web.law.duke.edu/cspd/publicdomainday/2026/), Duke, 1 January 2026.
- Cornell University Library, [Copyright Term and the Public Domain](https://guides.library.cornell.edu/copyright/publicdomain), undated.
- US Copyright Office, [Circular 33](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ33.pdf), revised March 2021.
- Scrivner et al., [Pandemic practice](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7492010), *Personality and Individual Differences*, 15 September 2020.
- Wikipedia, [Night of the Living Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_of_the_Living_Dead).
- Wikiquote, [Phantom of the Opera (1925)](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/The_Phantom_of_the_Opera_(1925_film)).

structuralLimitations: SERP: Firecrawl disconnected; 1 WebSearch (US-served index, not Google ranking). Top 5: purewow (2019), romper (2021), refinery29 (2020), the-line-up (2020, updated 2025), today.com. Weak in top 10: 3 (two hijacked-subdomain spam pages and a newswire press release), matching PLAN. None of the five mentions copyright or the public domain.

Prompt framing vs source: the prompt treats modern lines as a copyright problem, but Circular 33 says words and short phrases are uncopyrightable. The no-modern-quotes rule is BRIEF §6 editorial policy plus trademark and longer-script risk; the post says so plainly rather than overstating the law.

The 1 January 2027 date for Dracula and Frankenstein rests on Duke's 95-year rule (with its Mood Indigo 1931-to-2027 example) and Wikipedia stating 2027 for both films; I did not check each film's registration year in the Catalog of Copyright Entries (Duke notes an earlier registration year would control, as with Cimarron).

Exact wording of public-domain lines is from Wikiquote transcriptions (Nosferatu, Phantom 1925, Night of the Living Dead, Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde 1920, The Bat Whispers), not from watching prints; the post tells readers to check against their print. Wikiquote spells "Barbara"; the character is Barbra per Wikipedia, so the post uses Barbra. Nosferatu English intertitles are translations whose own copyright varies by restoration; the post says so. The Jekyll intertitle matches Dorian Gray (Gutenberg #174) verbatim.

Scrivner et al. 2020 is free to read under Elsevier's COVID-19 access licence via Europe PMC rather than a CC licence; full text read via the Europe PMC REST API. Batch 1's halloween-ideas-for-boyfriend cited "Scrivner et al. PAID 2020", possibly the same paper; caps are per batch and capcheck is clean.

Original lines were cross-checked for 5-word overlaps against all 55 sibling files in both batches (one collision with halloween-quotes was rewritten). The ItemList mirrors the five numbered film H3s; the five genre H3s are unnumbered groups and are not ranked.

Body sits at 1,796 words, close to the 1,800 cap: the 40 originals and 10 public-domain quotes take most of it. Cut from earlier drafts: Caligari (1920) and Hunchback (1923) entries, both verified public domain.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine asked which horror movie lines are safe to reuse, or when Dracula and Frankenstein enter the public domain, has a reason to cite this page: none of the five ranking lists mentions copyright, the 1 January 2027 date, or the Night of the Living Dead notice story, and this page dates each status to Duke, Cornell and the Copyright Office. For the plain "famous Halloween movie quotes" intent it is weaker than the incumbents, because it deliberately does not print the modern lines people search for; with today.com, purewow and refinery29 holding authority, expect the copyright long-tail to be the realistic win, not the head term.
